title: Drift Velocity and Current Density in Conductors
short_intro: Drift velocity is the average velocity attained by charged particles, such as electrons in a material, due to an electric field. It forms the microscopic foundation for macroscopic electrical conduction in metals.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of drift velocity, relation between current and drift velocity, Ohm's law verification via microscopic parameters, and factors affecting drift velocity.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Derivation of drift velocity from relaxation time, microscopic form of Ohm's law (J = sigma E), mobility of charge carriers, and temperature dependence of resistivity.

prerequisites: Thermal motion of electrons in metals

concept_notes.heading: Microscopic Origin of Current
bullets: In the absence of an electric field, free electrons in a conductor move randomly with thermal velocities of the order of 10<sup>5</sup> m/s, resulting in zero net current.
When an external electric field is applied, electrons experience an electrostatic force and acquire a slow net directional motion opposite to the field.
The magnitude of this drift velocity is extremely small, typically of the order of 10<sup>-4</sup> m/s under normal laboratory current conditions.

concept_notes.heading: Relaxation Time and Mean Free Path
bullets: During their drift, electrons undergo continuous collisions with the fixed positive ion cores of the metal lattice.
The average time interval between two successive collisions is called the relaxation time, denoted by the symbol τ.
The mean free path (λ) is the average distance traveled by an electron between successive collisions.

concept_notes.heading: Mobility of Charge Carriers
bullets: Mobility (μ) is defined as the magnitude of drift velocity per unit electric field.
It serves as a measure of how quickly a charge carrier can move through a metal or semiconductor under the influence of an electric field.
The SI unit of mobility is m<sup>2</sup>/V·s.

concept_notes.heading: Microscopic Form of Ohm's Law
bullets: Current density (J) is directly proportional to the applied electric field (E) inside a uniform conductor.
The constant of proportionality is the electrical conductivity (σ), expressed as J = σE.
This relation represents the local or microscopic form of Ohm's law, independent of the geometry of the conductor.

derivations.title: Derivation of Drift Velocity and Current Relation
derivations.conditions: Uniform conductor of cross-sectional area A, length l, and electron number density n.
steps: Consider an electric field E applied across the conductor, causing an acceleration a = eE/m for each electron of mass m and charge e.
The drift velocity v<sub>d</sub> is the average velocity gained between collisions, given by v<sub>d</sub> = aτ = (eE/m)τ.
The total number of free electrons in a segment of length v<sub>d</sub>Δt is N = n A v<sub>d</sub> Δt.
The charge passing through the cross-section in time Δt is ΔQ = Ne = n A e v<sub>d</sub> Δt.
The electric current I = ΔQ/Δt = n e A v<sub>d</sub>.

derivations.title: Derivation of Conductivity and Microscopic Ohm's Law
derivations.conditions: Free electron gas model in a metal under steady electric field E.
steps: Substitute the expression for drift velocity v<sub>d</sub> = (eE/m)τ into the current equation I = n e A v<sub>d</sub>.
We get I = n e A (eE/m)τ = (n e<sup>2</sup> τ / m) A E.
Current density J = I/A = (n e<sup>2</sup> τ / m) E.
Compare this with the microscopic Ohm's law J = σE to identify the conductivity σ.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Drift Velocity vs Electric Field
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A straight line passing through the origin with a positive slope equal to mobility μ on a v<sub>d</sub> versus E plot.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows that drift velocity is directly proportional to the applied electric field in standard metallic conductors.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently tested in conceptual multiple-choice questions regarding the linearity of carrier transport.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Resistivity vs Temperature for Metals
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A curve that starts near zero absolute temperature at a residual resistivity value and increases nearly linearly at higher temperatures.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: As temperature increases, thermal agitation of lattice ions decreases relaxation time τ, thereby increasing resistivity ρ.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Asked in PGT questions relating microscopic parameters to macroscopic temperature coefficients.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Current Density vs Electric Field (Microscopic Ohm's Law)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Linear plot of J versus E where the slope represents electrical conductivity σ.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Confirms obedience to microscopic Ohm's law for ohmic conductors.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Evaluates understanding of field-current density relationships.

solved_numericals.question: A copper wire of cross-sectional area 2 × 10<sup>-6</sup> m<sup>2</sup> carries a current of 3.2 A. If the free electron density of copper is 8 × 10<sup>28</sup> m<sup>-3</sup>, calculate the drift velocity of electrons.
solution_steps: Identify given values: I = 3.2 A, A = 2 × 10<sup>-6</sup> m<sup>2</sup>, n = 8 × 10<sup>28</sup> m<sup>-3</sup>, e = 1.6 × 10<sup>-19</sup> C.
Use formula: v<sub>d</sub> = I / (n e A).

solved_numericals.question: The relaxation time of free electrons in a metal is 2 × 10<sup>-14</sup> s. Find the mobility of electrons in the metal given that the mass of an electron is 9.1 × 10<sup>-31</sup> kg and its charge is 1.6 × 10<sup>-19</sup> C.
solution_steps: Identify parameters: τ = 2 × 10<sup>-14</sup> s, m = 9.1 × 10<sup>-31</sup> kg, e = 1.6 × 10<sup>-19</sup> C.

solved_numericals.question: A potential difference of 4 V is applied across a 2 m long metallic wire. If the mobility of electrons is 4.5 × 10<sup>-3</sup> m<sup>2</sup>/V·s, find the drift speed of the electrons.
solution_steps: Calculate electric field E = V / l = 4 V / 2 m = 2 V/m.
Use definition of mobility: v<sub>d</sub> = μ E.

assumptions_and_limitations: The Drude model assumes free electrons behave like an ideal gas and undergo instantaneous collisions with stationary ion cores, which neglects electron-electron interactions.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Drift velocity is the speed at which electric signals or current travel through a wire.
common_misconceptions.correct: Electric signals travel at a significant fraction of the speed of light, whereas drift velocity of electrons is extremely slow (~10<sup>-4</sup> m/s).
common_misconceptions.why: The electric field propagates nearly instantaneously through the conductor, setting all free electrons in motion simultaneously, which establishes current immediately.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Switching on a light switch causes an electron from the switch to reach the bulb instantly.
common_misconceptions.correct: Individual electrons drift very slowly; the energy is transmitted via electromagnetic field waves propagating through the circuit.
common_misconceptions.why: Drift speed is microscopic, but the coordinated movement of the sea of electrons driven by the electric field constitutes the electric current.

quick_revision: Drift velocity v_d is proportional to the applied electric field E and relaxation time τ.
Current in terms of Drift Velocity: I = n e A v_d
